summary: Defines a content feature schema, a profile of the media feature registration mechanisms, used to identify capabilities between extended Internet fax systems. It was replaced by RFC 2879.

eli5.summary: Before sending a fax, machines have to say what they can do, like color or size. This document defines the standard way to say it.

questions: how do fax systems negotiate capabilities
what are jbig and jpeg in fax
subtitle: Standard vocabulary for describing what Internet fax systems can send and receive.

tldr.problem: Internet fax systems have varying capabilities: some can handle color, others only black-and-white; some support high resolution, others do not. When two systems start to communicate, they need to negotiate which format to use, but there was no standard way to describe these capabilities.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2531 defines a content feature schema: a standardized vocabulary and syntax for describing the capabilities of Internet fax systems. Capabilities include image size and resolution, color support, compression schemes (MH, MR, MMR, JBIG, JPEG), media type, and paper size.
tldr.outcome: Fax systems can now describe their capabilities in a standard way, allowing senders to choose appropriate image formats for each receiver. RFC 2879 replaced this specification with improved feature descriptions.

today: RFC 2879 replaced this specification with an improved version of the content feature schema for Internet fax.

sections.title: Why Fax Capability Negotiation Matters
sections.content:
Extended Internet Fax describes fax systems that work over email and the Internet rather than traditional phone lines. Unlike traditional fax, which had a fixed set of capabilities defined by standards like Group 3 and Group 4 fax, Internet fax can vary widely: one system might support only black-and-white, 200 dpi images; another might handle full-color at 400 dpi.

When a sender wants to transmit a fax, they need to know what the receiver can handle. If the receiver cannot handle color but the sender transmits color, the receiver either drops the message or tries to convert it, losing quality. By having both systems describe their capabilities in a standard format, the sender can choose the right image format for each receiver.

This RFC defines the content feature schema for Internet fax: a standard syntax and vocabulary for expressing what an Internet fax system can do.
sections.eli5: Different fax machines have different abilities. One might handle colors, another might only handle black and white. We need to describe what each machine can do in a way everyone understands.

sections.title: The Feature Schema Framework
sections.content:
The feature schema is based on existing media feature registration mechanisms defined in other RFCs. It specifies a textual format for describing fax capabilities, using named feature tags with values that can be combined with logical operators (AND, OR).

For example, a simple fax system might be described as:

(& (color=Binary) (dpi=200) (image-file-structure=TIFF-S) (image-coding=MH) (paper-size=A4))

This means: the system supports black-and-white only (Binary color), 200 dots per inch resolution, TIFF-Simple file format, MH (Modified Huffman) compression, and A4 paper size.

A more complex system might support multiple options, expressed as:

(| (& (color=Binary) (image-coding=[MH,MR,MMR]) ) (& (color=Full) (image-coding=JPEG) ) )

This means: either black-and-white with one of three compression schemes, OR full color using JPEG.
sections.eli5: Capabilities are written like a recipe: 'I can handle black and white, 200 dots per inch, and MH compression'. OR means 'I can also handle color with JPEG'.

sections.title: Basic Fax Features
sections.content:
The schema defines feature tags for the fundamental characteristics of fax images:

Size and Resolution: Feature tags size-x and size-y indicate image dimensions in inches. The dpi tag indicates resolution in dots per inch. The dpi-xyratio tag handles cases where horizontal and vertical resolution differ (common in traditional fax).

Media Type and Paper: The ua-media tag indicates what kind of physical medium is supported: screen, stationery, transparency, envelope, or continuous roll. The paper-size tag specifies standard paper sizes: A4, A3, B4, letter, legal.

Color Capability: The color tag indicates the system's color support level: Binary (black-and-white only), Limited (a small fixed set of colors), Mapped (palette or indexed color), Grey (grayscale), or Full (continuous-tone color).

These basic tags allow a simple fax system to declare its capabilities. More advanced systems also declare support for multiple resolutions, color spaces, and encoding schemes.
sections.eli5: A fax system declares: what size papers it can handle, how fine the detail (dots per inch), whether it does black and white or color, and what kinds of compression it understands.

sections.title: Image Compression and Coding
sections.content:
The RFC defines several image coding schemes, inherited from traditional fax and modern standards:

Traditional Fax Compression:

  • MH (Modified Huffman): Basic one-dimensional run-length encoding, used by original Group 3 fax.
  • MR (Modified Read): Two-dimensional compression that improves on MH.
  • MMR (Modified Modified Read): Extended compression used by Group 4 fax.

Modern Compression:

  • JBIG (Joint Bi-level Image Group): Progressive bitplane compression, efficient for black-and-white images at varying resolutions.
  • JPEG (Joint Photographic Experts Group): Lossy compression for continuous-tone color and grayscale images.

A system may support one or more of these, depending on its design. The image-file-structure tag specifies how the coded data is wrapped (typically various TIFF profiles). The image-coding-constraint tag specifies how the compression is constrained for specific fax environments.

For JBIG compression, the JBIG-stripe-size tag controls how the image is divided into horizontal stripes for progressive transmission.
sections.eli5: Different compression methods squeeze fax images in different ways. Old methods like MH were simple but not very good. Newer methods like JPEG handle color but are more complex.

sections.title: Advanced Color Features
sections.content:
Systems with color capabilities declare additional details through color-specific feature tags. The color-levels tag specifies how many different color values each pixel can have. The color-space tag indicates the color model: Device-RGB (device-specific red-green-blue), Device-CMY (cyan-magenta-yellow for printing), Device-CMYK (with black), or CIELAB (a calibrated color space useful for color matching).

For systems using the CIELAB color space, additional tags describe the number of distinct values and the range (gamut) of colors that can be represented in each of the L*, a*, and b* color components. These details allow precise color reproduction across different devices.

A feature called Mixed Raster Content (MRC, governed by MRC-mode and MRC-max-stripe-size tags) allows advanced systems to represent documents as layers: a mask layer, a background layer, and a foreground layer. This is efficient for documents with both text and photographs, as the text can be encoded sharply at high resolution while the photograph uses lossy compression.
sections.eli5: Advanced systems describe exactly what colors they can show and how accurately. Some use standard color names, others use calibrated color values. MRC mode lets systems handle both sharp text and smooth photos in the same document.

sections.title: Capability Matching and Obsolescence
sections.content:
When two systems exchange fax documents, they match their capabilities using the feature schema. If a sender has a document available in multiple formats (black-and-white MH, color JPEG, etc.), the sender can match those formats against the receiver's declared capabilities and send the version the receiver can best handle.

The RFC includes detailed examples showing how different classes of fax systems (simple mode, high-end black-and-white, grayscale, full-color, and MRC-capable systems) describe themselves, and how the matching process works.

RFC 2879 replaced this specification, providing improved feature descriptions and clarifications for Internet fax systems.
sections.eli5: When two fax machines start talking, each says what it can do. The sender then picks the best format they both support. A newer document replaced this one with better rules.
